body.text: Victorians will head to the polls on November 28 to decide who will dictate policy in the state for the next four years.
Follow our live coverage below:

VEC forced to isolate votes after serious incident

The Victorian Electoral Commission has isolated sealed ballot boxes containing hundreds of votes from an early voting centre, after an "unauthorised individual" presented themselves as a VEC election casual on Wednesday.
In a statement, the Electoral Commissioner Sven Bluemmel said the individual had identified themselves to VEC staff as "someone trained and ready to work at the election".

"However, staff at the voting centre did not comply with the VEC's workforce protocols which require them to validate this claim by checking their letter of appointment with the venue roster," Bluemmel said."As a result, the individual, who had intended to work as a campaigner at the venue, was engaged to work inside the voting centre."

"However, staff at the voting centre did not comply with the VEC's workforce protocols which require them to validate this claim by checking their letter of appointment with the venue roster," Bluemmel said.
"As a result, the individual, who had intended to work as a campaigner at the venue, was engaged to work inside the voting centre."
The VEC said the individual had been under supervision and there was no suggestion that the integrity of the vote had been compromised.
Nevertheless as a precautionary measure, the sealed ballot boxes containing 700 in-district votes had been isolated and would be tracked into the count as a separate parcel of votes.

"This was a serious but isolated incident on a day that 212,000 Victorians participated actively in their democracy," Bluemmel said."I am disappointed this has occurred and we are committed to approaching this election transparently, and with the integrity that we, and Victorians, expect from us."

Carrie Bickmore appears with Jess Wilson for brain cancer funding promise
Media personality and Victorian Australian of the Year Carrie Bickmore has joined Opposition Leader Jess Wilson on the campaign trail today.

They're at The Brain Cancer Centre in Melbourne where Wilson has announced a Liberal-National government would direct $16 million over four years to a clinical trial known as BrainPOP (the Brain Perioperative Program).
It involves collecting samples from tumours to create individual profiles to guide specific treatments and to measure whether a therapy is proving effective.
The data on tumour biology to clinical outcomes is shared across multiple institutions.
Wilson says the fundings will allow the trials to be expanded.

"We see too many Victorians diagnosed with brain cancer," she says."One of the big problems with brain cancer is that it kills too many children, and we need to change the landscape when it comes to treatment options."
"We see too many Victorians diagnosed with brain cancer," she says.
"One of the big problems with brain cancer is that it kills too many children, and we need to change the landscape when it comes to treatment options."
Bickmore founded Beanies 4 Brain Cancer to raise money for research.

"When my late husband, Greg, was diagnosed with brain cancer there was not a clinical trial available for him," she says."To be honest, there was really no hope. Twenty-five years on from that diagnosis, survival rates haven't changed one bit."The only way this is going to change is with research and clinical trials."

"The only way this is going to change is with research and clinical trials."
Ken Smith from the Walter and Eliza Hall Institute of Medical Research says brain cancer is one of the hardest cancers to treat, with about 75 per cent of people dying within five years of diagnosis.
Key Event
🎞️: Richard Willingham buckles up with Ben Carroll
The ABC's state political reporter Richard Willingham is riding the Labor bus today, and had a chance during the trip to chat with his neighbour: Premier Ben Carroll.
Ben Carroll discusses how Labor is trying to genuinely win this election, their plans to stand up for working people, and why Victoria is "the best state in the greatest nation on Earth".
Liberals say volunteers should not be helping One Nation
The Liberal Party says its volunteers are "there to campaign for the Liberal Party, not other political parties" after a volunteer was snapped handing out how to vote cards for One Nation in Ivanhoe.
"We do not authorise anyone to distribute other parties' how-to-vote cards on our behalf," a party spokesperson said.

It’s probably worth noting that sometimes volunteers help each other out during toilet or coffee breaks — after hours standing next to each other, some people do build up relationships with their opponents.
Nonetheless, in a high-pressured election these little incidents can cause political headaches, especially when Labor has frequently accused One Nation and the Liberals of being in cahoots.
Expect plenty more of this.
Seats in focus: Mildura

While many rural Victorian seats have been dominated by conservatives from the Liberal and National parties or their predecessors, Mildura’s political history is a little more colourful. Labor won the seat twice in the mid-twentieth century although only for one term in both instances. After 30 subsequent years in the hands of the Country and National parties it was won by the Liberals in 1988. They were defeated in 1996 by independent Russell Savage in protest of their perceived neglect of rural Victoria while in government.

After the 1999 election, which produced a hung parliament, Savage was one of the three regional independents who backed Labor, which allowed Steve Bracks to form government. Savage held the seat for three terms before the Nationals reclaimed the seat. At the two subsequent elections the Nationals faced challenges from two separate independents. The second was Ali Cupper who in her second attempt at the seat as an independent, the third overall after first running as a Labor candidate, won the seat from the Nationals in 2018.

Cupper only managed to hold the seat for a single term before being ousted by the Nationals. Despite increasing her primary vote by about 3 percentage points and the Liberals splitting the Coalition vote, the Labor vote collapsed and there were not enough friendly preferences to win her the seat. She planned to contest this election but withdrew a few days before nominations closed, choosing to remain on Mildura council to which she was re-elected in 2024.
Carroll says 'more work to do' to stave off unemployment
Carroll is asked why Victoria is lagging behind the rest of the country when it comes to unemployment.
The national unemployment rate reached to 4.9 per cent in October, in data released by the Australian Bureau of Statistics yesterday, with Victoria recording 5.4 per cent.
It's tied with Tasmania for the highest in the country.

"I'm not a premier that blames external influences," he said."I know as the premier, we are the biggest procurer of jobs and services, we always have more work to do and that's what I'll always be focused on."
"I'm not a premier that blames external influences," he said.
"I know as the premier, we are the biggest procurer of jobs and services, we always have more work to do and that's what I'll always be focused on."
Carroll grilled over law and order
Premier Ben Carroll is being asked about an alleged kidnapping in Malvern East this week, when a mother and her daughter were allegedly taken from their home and held hostage overnight.
Media reports state that two people charged over the kidnapping were released on bail after their arrest.
Carroll is asked what he thought of the bail decision.
"I’m not a politician that will stand up here and tell the judges,” he said."It’s a matter for the independent judiciary."
"I’m not a politician that will stand up here and tell the judges,” he said.
"It’s a matter for the independent judiciary."
He is pressed on it, and admits the decision "didn’t meet [the] community’s expectations".

He reiterated his first call after becoming premier was to the Chief Commissioner of Police, and falls back into reciting Labor's policies on law and order, including Adult Time for Adult Crime sentencing laws.
Labor stands by decision to reverse purple bin mandate
Labor has stood by its decision to reverse its purple-lid glass recycling bin mandate, despite more than half the state's councils having rolled out the measure.
The policy would have required councils across the state to supply the bin to all homes by July next year, with the aim of reducing glass contamination in yellow mixed recycling bins.

Now the party's backflipped, joining the Coalition, Greens and One Nation in promising to overturn the mandate, meaning the regulations won't be compulsory regardless of which party is elected to government next weekend.
Economic development minister Anthony Carbines said expanding the state's container deposit scheme to include wine bottles means the household bin mandate can be removed.
"We can continue to divert from landfill and also save councils and residents money by not investing in an additional bin," he said.
But the City of Casey, in Melbourne's south-east, said it's frustrated the decision was made after it spent millions of dollars rolling out the bins.
"We do welcome Labor's announcement, but we felt that the timing where we've just rolled out the bins has not worked well," Casey mayor Michelle Crowther told 774 ABC Melbourne.
The Coalition has previously pledged to enforce a weekly general waste collection, instead of fortnightly in some areas, if elected to government.

"It is a big concern, again, a state government trying to mandate what a council should do without having discussions," Municipal Association of Victoria president Jennifer Anderson has previously said.
Coalition announces $16 million in brain cancer funding
The main health announcement from the opposition today is a pledge to invest $16 million over four years into brain cancer clinical trials.
The Coalition says it will support the expansion of the Brain Perioperative Program (BrainPOP), which tests new therapies for brain cancer.
It's one of the deadliest forms of cancer, with about 76 per cent of patients dying within five years of diagnosis.

"We want Victoria to lead the world in finding better treatments, giving patients access to the best medical research and clinical trials right here at home," Shadow Health Minister Georgie Crozier said.

"This $16 million investment will expand clinical trials, attract leading international research and give more Victorians, including those in regional communities, the opportunity to access potentially life-changing treatments."
BrainPOP is run by the Brain Cancer Centre at the Walter and Eliza Hall Institute.
Victoria stares down an approaching energy crisis
Under the Labor government, Victoria has been transitioning to renewable power as coal plants in the Latrobe Valley close.
But the transition is not coming fast enough.
Senior government officials have also warned that the state faces blackouts due to demand outstripping supply in 2028 when Yallourn, in Gippsland, ceases operations.
Experts have warned the state could face blackouts by 2028, as the Coalition ditches plans to build new transmission lines through rural Victoria.
The ABC's state political reporter Richard Willingham has more in this story:
Seats in focus: Melton

Melton has come to epitomise Labor’s decline in Melbourne’s outer-west. After more than 25 years of winning the seat on double-digit two-party preferred margins, Labor’s two-party vote dropped by almost 7 percentage points and its primary vote by 15 percentage points in what was otherwise a bumper election for the party in 2018. However, the Liberals also suffered a large primary vote fall, and the vote splintered across a large field of independents and minor parties. Both major parties saw some primary vote recovery at the 2022 election but Labor’s two-party preferred vote remained static.

With One Nation’s rise, the anti-establishment vote may now have a single brand to coalesce around after independents failed to seriously challenge Labor at the past two elections. While Melton is slightly more diverse than the average Victorian seat, its rates of higher education and property ownership are much lower than might be expected of a Liberal seat.
Bracks says the election isn't over until its over
Steve Bracks is asked about Ben Carroll's poor polling, and relates it to his own experience in 1999's state election, when he defeated Jeff Kennett.

"No-one gave me a chance to be premier, Kennett looked like he was a shoo-in," he said."There's still a week to go, it won't take that much more improvement in our primary vote for us to go very well at this election."
"No-one gave me a chance to be premier, Kennett looked like he was a shoo-in," he said.
"There's still a week to go, it won't take that much more improvement in our primary vote for us to go very well at this election."
When asked his thoughts on opposition leader Jess Wilson and her campaign, Bracks sidesteps the question.
"Why? Because I don't choose to have a perspective on that," he said.
Bracks backs Ben for a second term as premier
Former premier Steve Bracks has strongly backed Ben Carroll, saying Carroll has "all the qualities" to be a great second-term premier.
"I saw his development when Ben worked for me, I saw him as a minister, I saw him in government. He's a sensible middle-ground politician who is going to take Victoria forward," Bracks said.
Bracks is appearing alongside Carroll and Minister for Health Ingrid Stitt at Sunshine Hospital, helping to pitch Labor's case to voters in Melbourne's west.
He admitted Labor had a fight on its hands, but wanted to dispel notions Labor had abandoned its voter base.

"Nothing's safe, that's the current reality we're in … we can't take anything for granted," he said."I just wanted to attack this narrative that somehow Labor has neglected the west, it's just totally untrue."
"Nothing's safe, that's the current reality we're in … we can't take anything for granted," he said.
"I just wanted to attack this narrative that somehow Labor has neglected the west, it's just totally untrue."
Bracks was also asked about Carroll's predecessors, and admitted mistakes were made.

"I think Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan did a great job as premiers of this state," he said."Everyone makes mistakes, no-one is perfect. My government made mistakes, the Kennett government made tonnes."I think it's self-evident that there's issues there in relation to debt and relation to the Big Build."
"I think Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan did a great job as premiers of this state," he said.
"Everyone makes mistakes, no-one is perfect. My government made mistakes, the Kennett government made tonnes.
"I think it's self-evident that there's issues there in relation to debt and relation to the Big Build."
Two royal commission witnesses referred to Victoria Police
Two people who appeared before the Big Build royal commission this week, have been referred to Victoria Police.
Counsel Assisting Chris Carr SC didn't name the pair, but says they will now be considered for possible charges.

"The commission has today referred a number of matters arising from the evidence of witnesses this week, and has referred two people to Victoria Police for consideration of whether they ought to be prosecuted for any offences," he says.
The royal commission will not sit today, and instead will return for more public hearings on November 30.
Steve Bracks joins Labor's re-election campaign
Labor has brought in the big guns to rev up the campaign. Former premier Steve Bracks joins Ben Carroll on the trail, and he opens his remarks by saying "Labor does care about the west".

It’s a pointed comment given Labor is under immense pressure in Melbourne's western and northern suburbs, which have traditionally been safe seats. The feeling in those communities is that Labor has taken them for granted.
Ben Carroll speaks to RN Breakfast
Carroll was asked by presenter Sally Sara where he was going to find the money for Labor's healthcare promises, including the free dental clinics that have been announced.
Carroll says he's "cancelled gold plaques and pot plants" among more significant government savings.

"I've already made some difficult decisions around the Suburban Rail Loop, finding $2 billion in savings. I've delayed some level crossings, I've made savings in government agencies coming together," he says."Wherever I've been able to save a dollar, I have."

"I've already made some difficult decisions around the Suburban Rail Loop, finding $2 billion in savings. I've delayed some level crossings, I've made savings in government agencies coming together," he says.
"Wherever I've been able to save a dollar, I have."
The premier was also keen to paint a more positive picture of the current state of Victoria than his Liberal counterpart.
"We've just overtaken Sydney, Singapore and Berlin to be in the top three in the world for startups. Our NAPLAN results are the best in Victoria's history," he says.
Jess Wilson up early on RN breakfast
Liberal leader Jess Wilson was at Queen Victoria Market early this morning to speak to RN Breakfast's Sally Sara (and recommend a bratwurst).
She asked for some patience from Victorians if she wins the election next weekend.
"I can't fix everything overnight, I can't pretend that I can. It is going to take time but we have to start that change straight away and that's what my team is ready to do," she says.
Wilson was probed on her pledge to trim the public service, saying she would find "responsible and disciplined savings" to the tune of $22 billion if elected.

"We've seen the public service grow by 60 per cent over the past 12 years while population growth has only been 19 per cent.""We need to be ensuring that we guarantee those essential and frontline services. We need to fix the roads here and through those disciplined savings we'll be able to invest in the priorities Victorians need."
"We've seen the public service grow by 60 per cent over the past 12 years while population growth has only been 19 per cent."

"We need to be ensuring that we guarantee those essential and frontline services. We need to fix the roads here and through those disciplined savings we'll be able to invest in the priorities Victorians need."
She also confirmed the Coalition's commitment to privatise the Melbourne wholesale market if elected.
Welcome to the blog
Good morning and welcome to our coverage of the Victorian election campaign.
Labor and Liberals will be out and about again making media appearances, so we'll bring you all the big moments from the campaign trail.
Early voting continues, despite revelations of a major incident that required ballots to be isolated.
The Big Build royal commission will not hold hearings today, but two witnesses from hearings during the week have been referred to Victoria Police.
